title: Neural Network Configuration and Efficiency Underlies Individual Differences in Spatial Orientation Ability
authors: Aiden E. G. F. Arnold et al., 2013
research_question: Does variability in neural network configuration and efficiency relate to individual differences in spatial orientation accuracy?

participants.description: 13 healthy, right-handed volunteers (7 women, mean age = 21.77 years, age range = 18–36 years) with no psychiatric or neurological disorders and normal or corrected-to-normal vision. (Initially 16, 3 excluded for inability to recall landmark locations).
participants.recruitment: All participants provided written informed consent as approved by the local research ethics board (CHREB 22848).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Nine 1-min video clips of random passive movement in first-person perspective through a virtual city with four unique landmarks in a 5x5 rectangular grid of identical buildings. Three control clips of a virtual city with no unique landmarks in a similar 5x5 grid. (Figure 1)

Still images of landmarks from the virtual city, presented with a question asking participants to indicate whether the starting landmark (e.g., the building in central image) to get to the target landmark (i.e., the building on the right side) by following the shortest path was 'left' or 'right'. (Figure 2)

measures.instrument: Proportion of correct orientation decisions in a virtual city task
fMRI BOLD signal, analyzed with Partial Least Squares (PLS)

measures.construct: Global efficiency of resting-state brain networks
measures.instrument: Graph theory metric (inverse average shortest path length) computed from resting-state fMRI data

measures.construct: Closeness centrality of resting-state brain network nodes
measures.instrument: Graph theory metric (inverse average path length from a node to all others) computed from resting-state fMRI data

measures.construct: Brain activity correlated with orientation accuracy
measures.instrument: fMRI BOLD signal, analyzed with Behavior PLS

findings.consequent: Increased brain activity in precuneus, cerebellum, retrosplenial cortex (RSC), right lingual gyrus, right parahippocampal gyrus, right angular gyrus, left middle frontal gyrus, and left occipital gyrus (group-level core network)
findings.mechanism: These regions form a core network for processing spatial information, landmark recognition, and route planning during orientation decisions.
findings.quote: Dominant positive saliences—brain areas showing significant increased activity while making orientation decisions—with a BSR of 3.3 (p < .001)

findings.antecedent: Higher global efficiency within the task-defined resting-state network
findings.consequent: Higher accuracy in making orientation decisions
findings.mechanism: Increased global efficiency indicates a greater integrative and communicative capacity of the network to share information, supporting better orientation performance.
findings.quote: increased global efficiency within this network supported more accurate orientation decision-making.

mechanisms: Individual differences in the configuration of task-evoked networks (which brain regions are recruited) strongly relate to performance. High-performing individuals engage additional brain areas involved in spatial processing, conferring a behavioral advantage.

Topological variability in the capacity of brain networks to integrate information (measured by global efficiency and node centrality) contributes to the expression of behaviors and cognitive processes that rely on those networks.
Increased global efficiency indicates a greater integrative and communicative capacity of a network to share information, supporting better orientation performance.

Increased closeness centrality of specific nodes (e.g., hippocampus, SMG, primary motor cortex) indicates a greater ability for these regions to efficiently integrate information within the task network, facilitating spatial memory, imagery, and motor intentions.
moderators: Performance on non-spatial perceptual tasks (face identity, emotion recognition)
implementation_implications: Understanding neural network variability in spatial orientation could help identify early symptoms of neurodegenerative disorders like Alzheimer's disease, which are associated with topographical disorientation.

Future research could investigate how topological components of spatial orientation networks change in neurodegenerative disorders and whether these changes are indicative of clinical severity and predictive of further cognitive decline.

Cluster Peaks Correlated with High Accuracy in Making Orientation Decisions

limitations: The orientation decision task used is novel and has only been reported once before, requiring more research to clarify specific cognitive processes underlying orientation decisions.

Nodes within the task-related networks are only characterized by one measure of centrality (closeness centrality), while other topological properties (degree, motif fingerprint, betweenness centrality) could provide further insights.
The study is cross-sectional, limiting causal inferences about network development or changes over time.
